title: Wie klingt Deutsch? — Aussprache-Basics
explain_md:
German spelling is far more consistent than English — learn these rules once and you can read almost any German word aloud correctly.

| Letters | Sound like | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **ie** | long "ee" | **wie** ("vee") |
| **ei** | "eye" | **heißen** ("HY-sen") |
| **sch** | "sh" | **Deutschland** |
| **ch** | soft rasp, no English match | **ich** |
| **z** | "ts" | **zehn** |
| **w** | English "v" | **wie**, **woher** |
| **v** | English "f" | **von** |
| **ß** | "ss" | **heißen**, **groß** |
| **ä ö ü** | new vowel sounds, not decoration | **schön**, **Tschüss** |

Read the letters, not the English instinct: **w** is never "w", **v** is never "v".

examples.en: w sounds like an English v, and ei sounds like "eye" — "vee hyst doo"
ü needs rounded lips — say "ee", then round them without moving your tongue

drills.q: How do you pronounce the German "w", as in "wie"?
drills.why: German w is always an English v sound — wie is "vee", not "wee".

drills.q: What does "sch" sound like, as in "Deutschland"?
drills.why: sch is always one sound: "sh".
ei is always "eye" — the opposite of ie.
ie is always a long "ee" — the mirror image of ei.

options: A hard stop, like a glottal catch
drills.why: ß is just a shorthand for ss — heißen sounds exactly like "heissen" would.

title: heißen, sein, kommen — the first three verbs
explain_md:
Three verbs get you through your first conversation: **heißen** (to be called), **sein** (to be), and **kommen** (to come).

| | heißen | sein | kommen |
|---|---|---|---|
| ich | heiß**e** | bin | komm**e** |
| du | heiß**t** | bist | komm**st** |
| er/sie | heiß**t** | ist | komm**t** |

**sein is irregular** — bin/bist/ist has no pattern to learn, just memorise it. The other two follow the normal present-tense pattern: stem + ending.

The three questions that use them: **Wie heißt du?** (What's your name?), **Wer bist du?** (Who are you?), **Woher kommst du?** (Where are you from?) — and note **aus** for the answer: *Ich komme **aus** Kanada.*

drills.why: ich → heiße.
du → heißt.
ich → komme.
du → bist, irregular and worth memorising.

title: er, sie, es — standing in for a noun
explain_md:
Once you've named something, you don't repeat the noun — you use a pronoun, and which one depends on the noun's **gender**, not on real-world sex.

| article | pronoun | example |
|---|---|---|
| der | er | *Der Stuhl* → **er** ist schön |
| die | sie | *Die Lampe* → **sie** ist teuer |
| das | es | *Das Bett* → **es** ist neu |

A person follows the same rule: *Simon* → **er**, *Miriam* → **sie**. For more than one of anything, plural is always **sie**: *Die Kinder* → **sie** spielen.

examples.de: Der Stuhl ist schön. Er ist neu.
examples.en: The chair is beautiful. It's new.

examples.de: Die Lampe ist teuer. Sie kostet 40 Euro.
examples.en: The lamp is expensive. It costs 40 euros.

examples.de: Simon kommt aus der Schweiz. Er lernt Deutsch.
examples.en: Simon is from Switzerland. He's learning German.

drills.q: Der Tisch ist groß. ___ ist aus Holz.
drills.why: der Tisch is masculine → er.

drills.q: Die Uhr ist kaputt. ___ funktioniert nicht.
drills.why: die Uhr is feminine → sie.

drills.q: Das Handy ist neu. ___ war teuer.
drills.why: das Handy is neuter → es.

drills.q: Miriam wohnt in Berlin. ___ arbeitet dort.
drills.why: A woman's name takes sie regardless of article rules.

title: Present tense — regular verbs, all persons
explain_md:
Most German verbs are regular: drop **-en** from the infinitive, add the ending for the person.

| | wohnen | arbeiten* |
|---|---|---|
| ich | wohn**e** | arbeit**e** |
| du | wohn**st** | arbeit**est** |
| er/sie | wohn**t** | arbeit**et** |
| wir | wohn**en** | arbeit**en** |
| ihr | wohn**t** | arbeit**et** |
| sie/Sie | wohn**en** | arbeit**en** |

\*Stems ending in **-t** or **-d** (arbeiten, finden) get an extra **e** before the ending, so the consonants don't collide: *du arbeit**e**st*, not *arbeitst*.

**nicht** negates the whole idea, placed after the verb (and after the object, if there is one): *Ich arbeite **nicht** heute.*

drills.why: er/sie/es → wohnt.
wir → arbeiten.
du + stem ending in -t → the extra e: arbeitest.
A noun is negated with kein, not nicht.

title: mein, dein — and ja / nein / doch
explain_md:
**mein** (my) and **dein** (your) change their ending like *ein* does:

| | masc | fem | plural |
|---|---|---|---|
| ich | **mein** Onkel | **meine** Schwester | **meine** Eltern |
| du | **dein** Onkel | **deine** Schwester | **deine** Eltern |

Answering a question has three words, not two:

- **ja** — yes, to a normal question. *Ist das dein Vater? — **Ja**.*
- **nein** — no, to a normal question. *Sprichst du Englisch? — **Nein**.*
- **doch** — "actually, yes" — for a **negative** question you're contradicting. *Sprichst du nicht Deutsch? — **Doch**, ich spreche Deutsch.* Answering that with **ja** would sound like you're agreeing you *don't* speak German.

examples.de: Ist das nicht deine Mutter? — Doch!
examples.en: Isn't that your mother? — Yes, it is!

drills.why: der Bruder is masculine → mein.
die Tante is feminine → deine.

drills.q: Hast du keine Geschwister? Doch, ich habe...
drills.why: doch contradicts the negative — it means you DO have siblings.
The question isn't negative, so a plain yes is ja.

title: der, die, das
explain_md:
Every German noun has a **grammatical gender** — masculine, feminine or neuter — and it decides the article. It usually has nothing to do with real-world gender: *das Mädchen* (the girl) is neuter.

| | article | example |
|---|---|---|
| masculine | **der** | der Stuhl |
| feminine | **die** | die Lampe |
| neuter | **das** | das Bett |
| plural | **die** | die Stühle |

There's no reliable shortcut — gender is learned **with** the word, not worked out from it. That's why this course always shows you *der Stuhl*, never just *Stuhl*.

drills.why: Learned gender: der Tisch.
Learned gender: die Lampe.
Learned gender: das Regal.

drills.q: Plural of der Stuhl / die Lampe / das Bett all use:
drills.why: Every plural noun takes die, whatever its singular gender was.

title: nicht vs kein
explain_md:
Two ways to say "not", and which one depends on what follows.

**kein** negates a **noun** — anything you could put *ein* or nothing in front of: *Ich habe **kein** Handy.* *Ich sehe **keine** Brille.* It changes endings exactly like *ein* does.

**nicht** negates everything else — a verb, an adjective, a whole sentence: *Ich arbeite **nicht**.* *Das ist **nicht** teuer.*

Rule of thumb: could the sentence have used **ein / eine**? Then it's **kein**. Otherwise it's **nicht**.

drills.why: Kinder is plural — keine, negating the noun.
günstig is an adjective, not a noun — nicht.
die Brille is feminine → keine.
Negating the verb arbeiten → nicht.

title: Making plurals
explain_md:
German plurals don't follow one rule — they're learned per word, the same way gender is. But five patterns cover almost everything:

| pattern | example |
|---|---|
| -e | der Termin → die Termin**e** |
| -(e)n | die Lampe → die Lampe**n** |
| -er / ⁠umlaut | das Buch → die B**ü**ch**er** |
| -s (mostly loanwords) | das Handy → die Handy**s** |
| no change | der Drucker → die Drucker |

Whatever the singular's gender, the plural article is always **die**. That part, at least, never changes.

drills.why: Umlaut plus -e is the pattern for this word.
-e nouns usually add -n for the plural.
Loanwords usually just add -s.
die, regardless of the singular's gender.

title: The accusative — saying what you need
explain_md:
When a noun is the **object** of the sentence — the thing a verb is done to — masculine articles change. Feminine, neuter and plural stay exactly as they are.

| | subject | object (accusative) |
|---|---|---|
| masc | **der** / **ein** Drucker | **den** / **einen** Drucker |
| fem | **die** / **eine** Maus | unchanged |
| neut | **das** / **ein** Tablet | unchanged |
| plural | **die** Termine | unchanged |

*Ich brauche **den** Drucker.* *Ich suche **einen** Stift.* Three quarters of the table does nothing, which is the useful part: **der → den, ein → einen**, and everything else you already know.

drills.why: Masculine object → den.
das Passwort is neuter, unchanged in the accusative.
Masculine indefinite object → einen.
Feminine never changes in the accusative.

title: können — and where the second verb goes
explain_md:
**können** (can, to be able to) is a modal verb, and modal verbs work differently from every verb so far.

**ich and er/sie/es are identical — no ending:**
```
ich   kann      wir  können
du    kannst    ihr  könnt
er    kann      sie  können
```

**The other verb goes all the way to the end, as an infinitive:**
*Sie **kann** wirklich super **tanzen**.*
*Ich **kann** nicht gut **kochen**.*

This is the *Satzklammer* — the sentence bracket: können in slot two, the real verb waiting at the end. Everything in between (wirklich, super, nicht gut) sits inside the bracket.

drills.why: ich → kann, no ending.
du → kannst.
The infinitive stays at the very end.
wir → können.

title: The verb goes second — and am / um for time
explain_md:
In a German statement, the **finite verb is always the second element** — not necessarily the second word.

```
Ich      gehe   am Samstag ins Kino.
Am Samstag  gehe   ich ins Kino.
```

Move *am Samstag* to the front, and the verb still has to come right after it — the subject *ich* slides to third place instead. Getting this wrong (*Am Samstag ich gehe...*) is one of the most common early mistakes.

For time, two small prepositions do a lot of work: **am** for days (*am Montag*), **um** for clock times (*um vier Uhr*).

examples.de: Am Samstag gehe ich ins Kino.
examples.en: On Saturday I'm going to the cinema.

examples.de: Ich habe um vier Uhr Zeit.
examples.en: I have time at four o'clock.

drills.why: The verb must be the second element, so it comes right after Am Montag.
Days use am.
Clock times use um.
habe must sit in second position, right after Heute.

title: mögen, essen, möchte — talking about food
explain_md:
**mögen** (to like) is irregular in a specific way — the singular loses its g:
```
ich mag     wir mögen
du magst    ihr mögt
er mag      sie mögen
```

**möchte** (would like) is its own polite form, used for ordering and requests — never say *ich mag* to order food, that means "I like", not "I'd like":
```
ich möchte     wir möchten
du möchtest    ihr möchtet
```

**essen** changes its vowel for du/er: *ich esse, du **i**sst, er **i**sst.* Same pattern as *nehmen*: *ich nehme, du **nimm**st.*

drills.why: ich → mag, for a general preference.
möchte is the polite ordering form.
du → magst, for a general preference.
essen changes vowel for er: isst.

title: Separable verbs
explain_md:
Verbs like **ankommen** (to arrive) split in two: the prefix breaks off and travels to the **end of the sentence**, while the rest is conjugated normally in position two.

```
ankommen  →  Ich  komme  um sechs Uhr  an.
abholen   →  Holst du mich  ab?
einsteigen → Wir  steigen  in Hamburg  ein.
```

Common separable prefixes: **an-, ab-, ein-, aus-, um-, auf-, mit-**. In the dictionary they look like one word (*ankommen*), but in a sentence they never stay together.

examples.de: Ich komme um sechs Uhr an.

drills.why: an splits off and goes to the end.
After a modal (kannst), the separable verb stays whole at the end as an infinitive.
steigen stays in position two, um moves to the end.

title: Perfekt with haben — talking about the past
explain_md:
The everyday way to talk about the past in conversation: **haben**, conjugated, plus a **participle** at the end.

*Ich **habe** eingekauft.* *Was **hast** du gestern **gemacht**?*

**Regular verbs: ge- + stem + -t.**
machen → **gemacht** · kaufen → **gekauft** · aufräumen → **aufgeräumt**

**Separable verbs keep the prefix, with ge- squeezed in the middle:**
einkaufen → **ein**ge**kauft** · aufräumen → **auf**ge**räumt**

Two clauses joined by *und* share one **habe**: *Ich **habe** eingekauft **und** aufgeräumt* — no need to repeat it.

examples.de: Wir haben eine Pause gemacht und Zeitung gelesen.
examples.en: We took a break and read the newspaper.

drills.why: Regular: ge- + stem + -t.
The prefix ein- stays first, ge- slots in after it.
The participle is always last.

title: Perfekt with sein — going, flying, staying
explain_md:
Most verbs take **haben** in the Perfekt. A short list of verbs about **movement** — or a couple that just don't move — take **sein** instead.

**Movement from one place to another:**
fahren → *ich **bin** gefahren* · fliegen → *ich **bin** geflogen* · kommen → *ich **bin** gekommen*

**The odd one out — no movement, but still sein:**
bleiben → *ich **bin** geblieben*

Everything else — feiern, kaufen, machen — takes **haben**, same as before. The list of sein-verbs is short and worth learning by heart rather than guessing.

Germans also use the simple past of *sein* and *haben* even in speech, unlike other verbs: **war/warst/war** and **hatte/hattest/hatte**, for "was" and "had".

examples.de: Im Sommer bin ich nach Hamburg gefahren.
examples.en: In summer I went to Hamburg.

examples.de: Ich hatte Glück mit dem Wetter.
examples.en: I was lucky with the weather.

drills.why: fahren is movement, so it takes sein.
feiern isn't movement — haben, like most verbs.

drills.q: The exception that takes sein without moving:
drills.why: bleiben is the one worth memorising.
hatte is the simple past of haben, used even in speech.

title: Accusative — the object case
explain_md:
When a noun is the **object** of the sentence — the thing being acted on — masculine articles change. **Only masculine.**

| | subject (nom.) | object (acc.) |
|---|---|---|
| masc | **der** / **ein** Mann | **den** / **einen** Mann |
| fem | **die** / **eine** Frau | **die** / **eine** Frau |
| neut | **das** / **ein** Kind | **das** / **ein** Kind |
| plural | **die** Kinder | **die** Kinder |

```
Der Mann  →  Ich sehe  den Mann.
Ein Apfel →  Ich esse  einen Apfel.
Die Frau  →  Ich sehe  die Frau.     (unchanged)
Das Kind  →  Ich sehe  das Kind.     (unchanged)
```

So three quarters of the table does nothing. **Learn der → den and ein → einen and you have accusative.**

drills.why: Masculine object → den.
Masculine indefinite object → einen.
Feminine never changes in accusative.
Neuter never changes.
Hund is masculine and it's the object → einen.

title: Modal verbs — können, müssen, wollen
explain_md:
Modal verbs express ability, obligation and desire. Two things to know:

**1. ich and er/sie/es are identical** — no ending on either.
```
ich   kann      wir  können
du    kannst    ihr  könnt
er    kann      sie  können
```

**2. The other verb goes to the very end, as an infinitive.**
```
Ich  kann   Deutsch  sprechen.
Ich  muss   heute    arbeiten.
Ich  will   nach Hause  gehen.
```

This is the *Satzklammer* — the sentence bracket. The modal is in slot 2, the real verb waits at the end. It feels strange at first and then becomes automatic.

| | means |
|---|---|
| können | can, be able to |
| müssen | must, have to |
| wollen | want to |
| möchten | would like (polite) |
| dürfen | be allowed to |

drills.why: ich → kann, no ending.
er → muss, same as ich.
The infinitive goes to the very end.
du → kannst.

title: Saying where something is
explain_md:
The prepositions that answer **wo?** — and they all take the **dative**.

| | |
|---|---|
| **neben** | next to |
| **zwischen** | between |
| **gegenüber** | opposite |
| **bei** | at, near, at the house of |

*Die Bank ist **neben der** Post.*
*Der Park ist **zwischen dem** Bahnhof und **der** Schule.*

**zum** and **zur** are contractions you will use constantly: **zu dem → zum**, **zu der → zur**. Learn them as whole words for now — the dative underneath arrives in unit 29.

*Ich gehe **zum** Bahnhof.* (der Bahnhof)
*Ich gehe **zur** Post.* (die Post)

For directions you mostly need three words: **links**, **rechts**, **geradeaus**.

examples.de: Die Apotheke ist neben der Bank.
examples.en: The pharmacy is next to the bank.

examples.de: Gehen Sie geradeaus und dann links.
examples.en: Go straight on and then left.

examples.de: Der Park ist gegenüber der Schule.
examples.en: The park is opposite the school.

drills.why: zu + der = zur, for a feminine noun.
zu + dem = zum.
neben takes the dative and does not change form itself.

title: es gibt — there is, there are
explain_md:
**es gibt** means *there is* AND *there are*. It never changes.

*Es gibt **einen** Balkon.*
*Es gibt **zwei** Zimmer.*

Two things to notice.

**It takes the accusative.** That is unit 21 doing real work: *es gibt **einen** Supermarkt*, not *ein Supermarkt*.

**It stays singular.** English switches to *there are* for more than one; German does not. *Es gibt drei Zimmer* — still *gibt*.

To ask: ***Gibt es** hier einen Supermarkt?* — the single most useful question in a strange town.

drills.why: es gibt takes the accusative, so der Balkon becomes einen Balkon.
es gibt never becomes plural.
Verb first for a yes/no question.

title: The Perfekt with haben — talking about the past
explain_md:
This is how Germans talk about the past in conversation. Two pieces: **haben**, conjugated, and a **participle** at the end.

*Ich **habe** Brot **gekauft**.*
*Was **hast** du gestern **gemacht**?*

**Regular verbs: ge- + stem + -t.**
machen → **gemacht** · kaufen → **gekauft** · arbeiten → **gearbeitet**

**Strong verbs end in -en and often change the vowel.** There is no rule; they are learnt one at a time, and the common ones are worth knowing cold:

essen → **gegessen** · trinken → **getrunken** · sehen → **gesehen** · lesen → **gelesen** · schreiben → **geschrieben**

**Verbs ending in -ieren take no ge-**: studieren → *studiert*, telefonieren → *telefoniert*.

The bracket again: haben second, participle last.

examples.de: Was hast du am Wochenende gemacht?
examples.en: What did you do at the weekend?

drills.why: Regular: ge- + stem + -t.
Strong verb: -en ending and a vowel change.
Last. Always last.

title: The Perfekt with sein — going and becoming
explain_md:
Most verbs take **haben**. A short list takes **sein**, and you cannot mix them up without sounding wrong.

**Movement from one place to another:**
gehen → *ich **bin** gegangen* · fahren → *ich **bin** gefahren* · kommen → *ich **bin** gekommen* · fliegen → *ich **bin** geflogen*

**A change of state:**
aufstehen → *ich **bin** aufgestanden* · einschlafen → *ich **bin** eingeschlafen* · werden → *ich **bin** geworden*

**And three that just do:**
**sein** → *ich **bin** gewesen* · **bleiben** → *ich **bin** geblieben* · **passieren** → *es **ist** passiert*

The list is short and closed. Learn these, and use **haben** for everything else.

Note **bleiben** is the odd one — staying is the opposite of moving, and it still takes sein. That is the exception people remember.

drills.why: gehen is movement, so it takes sein.
kaufen is not movement — haben, like most verbs.

drills.q: Which takes sein even though nothing moves?
drills.why: bleiben is the exception worth memorising.

title: am, um, im — when something happens
explain_md:
Three prepositions, chosen by the **kind** of time word. Learn them as a set; picking between them is not a judgement call.

| | for | example |
|---|---|---|
| **am** | days, parts of the day | am Montag, am Abend |
| **um** | clock times | um acht Uhr |
| **im** | months, seasons, years | im Januar, im Sommer |

Two exceptions worth knowing on day one:

**in der Nacht** — not *am*. The night is the odd one out.
**Am Wochenende** for the weekend as a whole.

And no preposition at all with **heute, morgen, gestern**: you say *morgen* and *heute Abend*, never *am morgen* for tomorrow.

examples.de: Der Kurs beginnt um neun Uhr.

drills.why: am for days of the week.
um for clock times, always.
im for months and seasons.
heute, morgen and gestern stand alone.

title: Adjectives after sein — the easy half
explain_md:
After **sein**, an adjective takes **no ending at all**. None. Whatever the gender, whatever the number.

*Der Tisch ist **groß**.*
*Die Lampe ist **groß**.*
*Das Fenster ist **groß**.*
*Die Fenster sind **groß**.*

One form, four sentences. This is the half of German adjectives that is easier than English.

**The other half is not, and it is not A1.** Put the adjective *before* the noun — *der große Tisch* — and it takes an ending that depends on gender, case and which article is in front of it. That is a B-level table and this course does not pretend otherwise.

So: describe things with **sein** and you can say almost anything. *Das Auto ist rot* rather than *das rote Auto*, until much later.

drills.why: After sein there is never an ending, whatever the gender.
Plural changes nothing. Still no ending after sein.
Predicative — after sein. The other two need adjective endings, which are not A1.
